label: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017
output:
Peter, I want to push back on this one, and I want to do it respectfully, because you’re not wrong about the underlying risk. Nine years in payroll means you’ve seen the mess up close, and some of what you describe is exactly why informal advances are dangerous. But I think the conclusion — close the window, give people notice, point them at the SACCO, and they’ll adjust — is where our experience seriously diverges. Brenda, since you’re going into the 18th, I’m going to put our numbers down, because I think they’ll help you more than my opinion will.

We did what you suggested, Peter. Almost word for word. We’re a logistics company, about 340 staff, depots in Embakasi and Changamwe, mostly drivers, turn-boys, loaders and warehouse clerks. We closed advances in February 2025 after Finance pushed back with the same arguments: we’re not a bank, it messes up the cash flow forecast, some people are on it every month. We gave two months’ notice and ran one financial literacy session with the SACCO. We thought we were doing it properly.

In the six months after we closed, debt collector and loan app calls to the office went from a handful to 61 logged by reception. Not 61 calls to the individuals’ phones — 61 calls to the office. Some of the apps were calling supervisors who had been listed as “referees.” That is a workplace problem, not just a personal finance problem. Unplanned absence on the two days after month-end also rose. Our fleet manager linked at least three missed Mombasa runs to drivers who were, in his words, “sorting out” loans. I can’t put a clean invoice number on that, but those costs are real and they spread across fleet, operations, reception and HR. They don’t sit neatly in one budget line, which is exactly why they get ignored in these meetings.

The reason isn’t that people are irresponsible. It’s timing and affordability. SACCO loans take two to three weeks to process and need guarantors. That is useless to a parent whose child has been sent home from school over fees on a Tuesday. At KES 28,000 a month, there is only so much emergency affordability to plan around. So people go to the apps. We had a loader at Changamwe who had six apps going at once by the time he came to me, borrowing from one to pay the other. It took us four months with payroll to unwind it. That was a cost we paid anyway — just in a worse form, at a higher price, and with the company’s supervisors being phoned in the middle of the day.

So we reopened in September 2025, but not as the old informal scheme. The old scheme was exactly what you’re warning against: discretionary, no written limit, come to my office and explain. The new one is a written policy. Maximum 40% of net pay, once per pay cycle, repaid in full at the next payroll, no fee, request through the payroll portal rather than my office. Before approving, we check total deductions against the Employment Act limit of two-thirds of wages. Nobody ends up with nothing at month end. That’s the part I’d underline for Brenda: the 40% cap is not the only control; it sits under the statutory deduction check.

Since reopening we’ve had about 55 to 70 requests a month, average around KES 9,000. We have recovered 100% except for two leavers, with total write-offs of roughly KES 14,000 for the year. I’m not pretending that’s zero, but compare it with 61 collection calls, supervisors being used as referees, rising absence after month-end and three missed Mombasa runs. Our Finance Manager now defends the scheme himself, because the forecast impact is known in advance. It’s a fixed ceiling, not a surprise. He can see the maximum exposure. He couldn’t see the cost of a driver missing a run because a loan app was calling him.

On your specific points, Peter: you say advances teach people to live on next month’s money. I agree that an uncapped, every-month advance does. A 40% cap, once per cycle, repaid in full at next payroll, is a different product. It’s a payroll timing facility, not a loan book. If someone is on it every month, the portal shows it and we can have a conversation. We don’t hide it. You say HR becomes the lender of first resort. In the old informal scheme, yes. In the new one, HR isn’t deciding who gets money; payroll is applying a rule. The portal does the routine work. My time went down, not up. The informal version was the time sink.

You say good luck recovering when someone leaves owing you. We recovered all but two leavers, and the write-off was about KES 14,000 for the year. That is not nothing, but it is a number Finance can forecast. And it’s smaller than the cost of the alternative we actually tried. You say there are SACCOs and banks. We refer people to the SACCO, and we do financial literacy. But a SACCO loan in two to three weeks with guarantors doesn’t solve a Tuesday emergency, and banks won’t lend at these amounts. The mobile apps will, at a price, and they call the workplace. That’s the part I’d ask Finance to weigh: the company is already in this business, just not on the balance sheet.

I also agree with you that financial literacy is useful. We do it. But one session with the SACCO is not an emergency loan. It helps people avoid the worst products; it doesn’t create cash for school fees on a Tuesday. Pretending otherwise is how you end up with a policy that looks clean in the meeting and messy on the shop floor.

Brenda, for the 18th, here’s the shape of what you could propose. It gives Finance the ceiling and the control they want, and it gives staff a bridge that doesn’t involve a loan app calling their supervisor.

- Put it in writing. Call it a salary advance or payroll timing facility, but make it a policy, not a favour. Eligibility after probation, not during notice, no side deals.
- Cap it at 40% of net pay. You could start lower, say 30%, and review after two quarters. Once per pay cycle, no top-ups while one is outstanding, repaid in full at the next payroll, no fee.
- Check the total deductions against the Employment Act two-thirds limit before approving. That’s the safeguard that stops someone walking away with nothing at month end.
- Move the request route to the payroll portal or a standard form, not your office. Approval should be rule-based: payroll/HR checks eligibility and the deduction limit; Finance gets a monthly schedule and a maximum exposure figure. No discretion, no “come and explain.”
- Report monthly: total advanced, recovery rate, write-offs, collection calls to the office, unplanned absence after month-end, missed runs. Review after two quarters. If the numbers go bad, you tighten the cap. That’s a much stronger position than arguing from principle.
- Keep the financial literacy and SACCO referral alongside it, not instead of it.

Peter, I’m not trying to pick a fight. If Brenda walked in and said “ignore Finance,” that would be bad advice. But our experience says closing the window doesn’t remove the need. It moves it to loan apps, to reception, to supervisors’ phones and to the shop floor. The company still pays, just in absence and missed runs and staff time. I’d rather pay it in a controlled payroll deduction with a ceiling Finance can forecast. That’s the case I’d make on the 18th, and I’d make it with the numbers, not a feeling. Good luck, Brenda.
